title: How Much Practice Do Students Need?
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Kane addresses the classic math-teaching frustration -- students can perform a skill in class but appear to have forgotten it entirely the next day -- by reframing the goal of practice around long-term memory rather than same-lesson performance. His answer to the titular question is concrete: students need enough practice that they can reliably retrieve a skill the following day, at which point practice can taper to smaller-scale retrieval maintenance. He acknowledges the practical objection that teachers don't have five to ten extra minutes per class to build in retrieval checks, and offers two structural responses: dedicating opening class time to prior-skill checks, or his own preferred fix, restructuring a year's curriculum around a small number of major strands taught in parallel all year (rather than six sequential units) so spaced practice is built into the architecture of the course rather than bolted on. He grounds the piece in the idea that skills sit in interconnected knowledge webs rather than isolated islands, so students who already have related prior knowledge need less repeated practice, while students without those connections need more. Kane closes by rejecting the common instructional-design orthodoxy that every lesson must serve exactly one objective, arguing that idea is inconsistent with how memory and learning actually work.
points: Kane's operational definition of 'enough practice' is retrieval-based, not performance-based: continue practicing a skill until students can reliably retrieve it the next day, then taper to smaller-scale spaced retrieval.

His preferred structural fix is curriculum redesign -- teaching several major strands in parallel throughout the year (rather than one unit at a time) so that spaced, interleaved practice is built into the course architecture instead of requiring extra bolted-on time.

He frames skill retention through a knowledge-web model: students with related prior knowledge can lean on that connection and need less repeated practice, while isolated skills require far more repetition to stick.

Kane explicitly pushes back on the common instructional norm that every lesson must have exactly one objective, arguing that this convention is 'not consistent with how humans learn' once you accept that learning is a change in long-term memory measured across days.
quotes: This is the answer to the titular question. How much practice do students need? Enough that they can reliably retrieve the skill the next day. Learning is a change in long-term memory, and the best practical way to measure long-term memory is to wait a day and see what students remember.
I took the toughest topics, the ones that students typically have the most trouble with, and stretched them out through the entire year.

Many teachers and schools are strongly committed to the idea that every lesson must have exactly one objective, and every part of the lesson must be in service of that objective. I think we should let go of that idea. It simply is not consistent with how humans learn.
A helpful mental model here is that the skills we want students to learn are part of webs of knowledge, not isolated islands.
In too many math classes those final few students watch the class move on before they’re ready, over and over again. Eventually they lose confidence as they feel like they just can’t keep up.
